summary: The CDNI Metadata interface lets interconnected content delivery networks exchange the content distribution metadata needed for acquiring and delivering content. This proposed standard gives a downstream CDN enough information to serve content on behalf of an upstream CDN.

plainLanguage.summary: When one delivery company handles packages for another, it needs instructions for each item. This defines the instruction sheet the companies share.

subtitle: The shared instruction sheet a downstream CDN fetches to know how to acquire, protect and deliver another CDN's content.

tldr.problem: When one CDN serves content on behalf of another, the downstream CDN needs per-content policy: where to fetch it, who may receive it, and how to cache it.
tldr.mechanism: The upstream CDN publishes I-JSON metadata objects over HTTP. A HostIndex leads to per-host and per-path metadata, which carry GenericMetadata objects for sources, access control, authorization, caching and grouping.
tldr.outcome: A downstream CDN can serve content in line with the upstream CDN's policy, and must refuse content whose mandatory-to-enforce metadata it cannot enforce. RFC 8006 is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8006 is a Proposed Standard and, according to the metadata for this site, has not been obsoleted or updated. Further metadata types and Auth methods are meant to be defined in separate documents.

sections.title: Why CDNs Share Metadata
sections.content:
Content Delivery Network Interconnection (CDNI) lets a downstream CDN (dCDN) service content requests on behalf of an upstream CDN (uCDN). The CDNI Metadata interface (MI) is one of five interfaces that can be combined into a CDNI solution. The metadata gives the dCDN enough information to handle requests in line with the uCDN's policies.

The RFC defines three things: a data structure that maps content and redirection requests to metadata objects, an initial set of GenericMetadata objects, and an HTTP web service for transferring them. The dCDN uses the metadata to process redirection requests received over the Request Routing Redirection interface and content requests received directly from User Agents.

Only a small initial set of capabilities is covered: acquisition source, delivery access control (location, time window, delivery protocol), delivery authorization and cache control. The design is extensible for future additions, and it only supports delivery over HTTP/1.1, and acquisition over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/1.1 over TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Two delivery firms work together. The first one writes down the rules for each parcel so the second one can deliver without phoning every time.

sections.title: Design Principles and the Object Model
sections.content:
Five objectives drive the design: cacheability of metadata objects, a deterministic mapping from requests to metadata, support for DNS redirection and application-specific redirection such as HTTP redirection, minimal duplication, and reuse of existing protocols. HTTP provides transport and caching, and I-JSON provides encoding.

The object model groups properties first by hostname and then by URI path. A HostIndex holds HostMatch objects. Each HostMatch contains one HostMetadata object. HostMetadata holds the default GenericMetadata for the host and zero or more PathMatch objects. A PathMatch holds one PatternMatch and one PathMetadata, which can in turn hold more PathMatch objects for more specific paths.

Any object that contains another may instead include a Link with a URI for it. That lets one object be fetched and stored once even if many hosts or paths reference it.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a filing cabinet. The top drawer is sorted by shop name, inside each shop folder are smaller folders for aisles, and a folder can just say 'see the folder over there' instead of copying it.

sections.title: Structural Objects and Override Rules
sections.content:
The HostIndex hosts array is evaluated in order, and the first HostMatch that matches the request MUST be used. A HostMatch host is an endpoint, and matching is done on the lowercase form. HostMetadata and PathMetadata each have a metadata array of GenericMetadata and optional paths; PathMatch objects are evaluated in order, and only the first match is used.

A PatternMatch has a pattern with two wildcards: the asterisk matches any sequence of characters, including none, and the question mark matches exactly one character. Three literals are escaped with a dollar sign as the escape character, giving $$, $* and $?. A case-sensitive flag defaults to false.

HostMetadata and PathMetadata form an inheritance tree. A GenericMetadata object of a given type overrides any object of the same type defined by a parent, and is otherwise inherited. A single object MUST NOT hold two GenericMetadata objects of the same type; a receiver ignores all but the first.

With DNS-based redirection only the hostname is known at request routing time, so a dCDN cannot evaluate PathMetadata. It SHOULD still check it for unsupported mandatory-to-enforce metadata before accepting the redirection.
sections.plainLanguage: Each shop has house rules, and an aisle can replace one rule for itself. If the aisle says nothing about a rule, the shop's rule still applies.

sections.title: Mandatory-to-Enforce and Redistribution
sections.content:
Every GenericMetadata object has three flags. mandatory-to-enforce defaults to true: if the dCDN does not understand or support such a property, it MUST NOT serve the content. safe-to-redistribute defaults to true and says whether the metadata can pass unchanged to another CDN. incomprehensible defaults to false and is set to true by a CDN that could not properly understand or transform metadata that is not safe to redistribute.

A transit CDN (tCDN) MUST NOT change mandatory-to-enforce or safe-to-redistribute, and can set incomprehensible to true but never back to false. A CDN MUST NOT use metadata marked incomprehensible by a uCDN.

The RFC spells this out in two tables. For a tCDN, an unsupported but mandatory property means it must not serve; if it also is not safe to redistribute, the tCDN sets incomprehensible when redistributing. For a dCDN, mandatory-to-enforce metadata that is incomprehensible, or not understood, means it must not serve.
sections.plainLanguage: Some instructions say 'you must follow this or do not deliver at all'. If a helper cannot follow such an instruction, it must hand the parcel back, and must never pretend it understood.

sections.title: The Initial GenericMetadata Objects
sections.content:
SourceMetadata lists sources in order of preference. Each Source has endpoints (all equal), a protocol and an optional acquisition-auth.

Three access-control lists are separate objects: LocationACL (footprints of type ipv4cidr, ipv6cidr, asn or countrycode), TimeWindowACL (windows with start and end as seconds since the UNIX epoch) and ProtocolACL. In each, the first matching rule decides, no listed rule matching means deny, and a missing list means allow all. A rule's action defaults to deny. The dCDN MUST take the logical AND of all the ACLs.

DeliveryAuthorization lists Auth methods, and a request is authorized if any one is satisfied. The RFC defines no Auth methods itself. Cache can exclude a path pattern from cache keys and choose which query-string parameters count, with an empty list meaning all are ignored. Grouping carries a ccid content collection identifier, for example for logging aggregation.
sections.plainLanguage: The sheet has boxes: where to fetch the parcel, which towns, hours and delivery methods are allowed, a password rule, how to file it in the warehouse, and a group label.

sections.title: The Metadata Interface
sections.content:
The interface is built on HTTP web services. Servers MUST support GET and HEAD, and responses with a body SHOULD include an ETag. Clients MUST NOT assume anything about URI structure. Objects are I-JSON with lowercase property names, sent as media type application/cdni with a CDNI Payload Type such as MI.HostIndex in the ptype parameter.

The dCDN is configured with the URI of the uCDN's HostIndex, which is the bootstrap. It GETs the HostIndex, matches the requested host, fetches any linked HostMetadata, and then recursively fetches matching PathMetadata. If it cannot retrieve all the metadata it needs, or it is stale and cannot be revalidated, the dCDN MUST NOT serve the content.

For versioning, the Payload Type identifies the specification, and a new version of a nested object requires new Payload Types for the outer objects too (for example MI.HostIndex.v2). Clients SHOULD send an Accept header with the Payload Type they expect. New GenericMetadata types must register a Payload Type, define their properties, and describe their security and privacy consequences.
sections.plainLanguage: The second company starts with one address it was given, reads the first page, and follows the 'see page X' notes until it has everything needed for this parcel. If a page is missing, it does not deliver.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
False metadata from an impersonated or malicious metadata server could deny service, point the dCDN at malicious origin servers, or remove delivery restrictions such as the ACLs, risking license violations and delivery costs. A malicious client could overload the metadata server or learn origin details and content restrictions. Metadata also reveals origin and policy information, and a content provider concerned about dCDNs learning usage patterns can tell its uCDN not to use CDNI.

Implementations MUST support TLS and MUST use it, with authentication of the remote end, between uCDN and dCDN. Alternatives such as an IPsec tunnel or a physically secured internal network between CDNs of the same corporate entity are allowed. General TLS guidance in RFC 7525 MUST be followed.
sections.plainLanguage: The instruction sheets are secret and must not be forged. So both companies check each other's identity and talk in a locked envelope.
